newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia opposition calls for keeping aid squeeze on.
newsitem.headline: Zambia opposition calls for keeping aid squeeze on.

text.p: Former president Kenneth Kaunda urged Western donors on Thursday to keep an aid squeeze on Zambia, saying it was the only peaceful form of protest against the excesses of the current government.

"We thank the donors for refusing to give these people money until they behave properly. The donors must maintain this stance if political protest is to remain non-violent," diplomats quoted Kaunda as saying.
Western governments resolved to lift a year-long aid squeeze on Zambia in early July, saying they were satisfied with its economic and governance record.

Donors led by the United States had cut aid to the southern African country in mid-1996 in protest against electoral reforms that banned some candidates, including Kaunda, from contesting presidential elections last November.
Seven parties subsequently boycotted the elections, which President Frederick Chiluba won by a landslide.
Kaunda said on Thursday the government had stepped up a campaign against the opposition and was vandalising public property to make it appear as if the opposition was responsible.

"We know what the MMD (ruling Movement for Multiparty Democracy) is driving at. They want to destabilise UNIP (opposition United National Independence Party). They are looking for an excuse to declare a state of emergency and ban UNIP," he said.
Three fires have destroyed public property in the capital this week.
The first, on Sunday night, was ignited by police in an operation to destroy illegal vendors' stalls in the city centre.
A second gutted part of a government building housing the vice president's office, while a third destroyed dozens of vendors' stalls at a market near the city centre.
Scores of vendors rioted in the central business district on Monday and Wednesday in protest against the burning of their stalls. Many lost all their merchandise.
State House said on Wednesday investigations had revealed that Kaunda and other opposition leaders were behind the three fires.
He dismissed the allegations as malicious.

"We in UNIP are consoled by the fact that the grieving citizens who have lost their only source of livelihood have not accepted such cheap lies. They know their property was burnt, not by UNIP, but by the MMD government itself," he said.
